newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Foreign firms worry over new Philippine mine rules.
newsitem.headline: Foreign firms worry over new Philippine mine rules.

text.p: Foreign mining companies represented by the Manila-based International Mining and Exploration Committee (IMEC) have called on the Philippines for clear mining regulations favourable to foreign investment, the organisation's president told Reuters on Wednesday.
IMEC has stated its case in a position paper.
"This document aims to present the concerns of the foreign mining community to the government," Robert Guest, who is also president of Chase Minerals (Philippines) Corp, said.
Guest was in Hong Kong attending the Asia Gold Congress.
"The document reiterates that profitability of the Philippine mining industry is essential for foreign investment," he said.

The Philippine Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) is to hold its fourth public hearing this Friday on fresh, more environmentally-friendly rules and regulations implementing the country's Mining Act passed in June 1995, Guest said.
"There is a concern that the legislation will be modified to the point of being inappropriate and impractical," the document says.

The Marcopper Mining Corp mine accident in March this year whipped up environmentalists' outrage, leading to a review of the Implementing Rules and Regulations (IRR) of the country's mining law, Guest said.
"The review has opened up a can of worms," he said.

Foreign mining firms worry the new rules will stifle business opportunities, for example by slapping what amounts to a 10 percent royalty on mining and milling costs - revenue that would go towards rehabilitating the environment.
"That's a killer, the industry will not develop," Guest said, noting that the Philippines had to remain competitive to attract investment and lure foreign money away from countries like Indonesia.

Foreign mining companies struggling for access to exploration land in the Philippines could become discouraged by a lack of approvals, Guest said, noting that since the Mining Act was signed last June no deals (known as Financial or Technical Assistance Agreements or FTAAs) had been signed.
Part of the problem lay in the government's organization, Guest said.
"The DENR is an umbrella organization which controls forestry, environment, land as well as the Bureau of Mines," Guest said, adding there was bound to be an inter-departmental conflict of interest.

According to the IMEC document, entitled "The Philippine Mining Industry, An International Perspective," foreign investment in exploration and feasibility studies alone could jump to US$154 million in 1997, up from a projected US$46 million in 1996.
Vice chairman of Philippine company Itogon-Suyoc Mines, Inc., J. Ernesto C. Villaluna, said the country welcomed foreign investors who were serious about mining.
"But we don't want them to make a mockery of our laws, we don't want speculators," said Villaluna, who is also vicepresident of the gold sector at the Philippine Chamber of Mines.
"The concern is that certain foreign mining companies just file blanket applications for much bigger areas than is allowed," Villaluna said, but declined to specify which firms.
Under an FTAA agreement, a single foreign firm can contract 81,000 hectares of land, Villaluna said.
"The foreign firms will also have to comply with capitalisation laws, where they have to inject a minimum amount," he said.
Villaluna was also attending the Asia Gold Congress in Hong Kong.
